ADVERTISING AND RECRUITING FOR WORKERS DURING A STRIKE OR LOCKOUT (LABOR CODE §§ 973-974; PEOPLE V. SMITH; UNEMP. INS. CODE § 1259; BELKNAP V. HALE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, collects the published legal materials that govern one narrow situation: the recruiting of workers for a shop, plant, or establishment at which a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute is already under way. It is organized around California Labor Code sections 973 and 974, which sit in the Labor Code chapter headed "Solicitation of Employees by Misrepresentation"; around People v. Smith, the published California decision construing section 973; and around the Unemployment Insurance Code and federal provisions that address the same situation from the side of the person being recruited. It states what those authorities say, in their own words where the words matter. It does not evaluate any advertisement, solicitation, offer, or hiring decision made by Acme, Inc. or by anyone else, does not say whether any particular work stoppage at 350 South Thomas Street, Pomona, California is or is not a strike, lockout, or trade dispute within the meaning of any of these provisions, and does not predict how any agency or court would rule. Each authority clause carries a gap note recording what was verified, against which publishers, and what was not resolved.

LABOR CODE SECTION 973 - AFFIRMATIVE DUTY TO DISCLOSE THE DISPUTE WHEN SOLICITING WORKERS
Labor Code section 973 imposes an affirmative disclosure duty on a person who seeks workers while a labor dispute is under way. By its terms the duty attaches to a person who advertises for or seeks employees "by means of newspapers, posters, letters, or otherwise," and equally to a person who solicits or communicates "by letter or otherwise" with persons to work for him, for the person he is acting for, or at any shop, plant, or establishment. The triggering condition stated in the section is that a strike, lockout, or other trade dispute "is still in active progress" at that shop, plant, or establishment. Where the condition is met, the section directs that the person "shall plainly and explicitly mention" in the advertisement or in the oral or written solicitation or communication that a strike, lockout, or other labor disturbance exists. The section states a duty to disclose; it does not, in its text, prescribe any particular wording, typeface, placement, or prominence for the disclosure, and it does not say who bears the burden of showing that a dispute was or was not in active progress.

LABOR CODE SECTION 973 - NAMING THE ADVERTISER AND THE PRINCIPAL, AND THE PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE RULE
Section 973 does not stop at the disclosure of the dispute. Its second sentence separately directs the person inserting the advertisement, solicitation, or communication - in a newspaper, on a poster, or otherwise - to insert his own name in it, and, if he is representing another, the name of the person he is representing and at whose direction and under whose authority he is inserting it. The third sentence attaches an evidentiary consequence to that name: its appearance in connection with the advertisement, solicitation, or communication "is prima facie evidence as to the person responsible for" it. On the face of the section, the identification requirement is written without its own triggering language, so the text alone does not settle whether it applies to every solicitation the section reaches or only to those made while a dispute is in active progress. The statute does not say what showing rebuts the prima facie evidence it creates, and does not address advertisements placed by a staffing agency, recruiter, or advertising intermediary in terms.

TWO DIFFERENT DUTIES IN ONE CHAPTER - SECTION 970(D) FORBIDS A FALSE STATEMENT, SECTION 973 REQUIRES A STATEMENT
Sections 970 and 973 sit in the same Labor Code chapter and both speak to labor disputes, but they operate differently. Section 970 prohibits influencing, persuading, or engaging a person to change residence for work "through or by means of knowingly false representations" about any of four listed subjects, the fourth of which, subdivision (d), is the existence or nonexistence of a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute affecting the work and pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last engaged in that labor. Section 970 is therefore addressed to what is said: it is violated by a knowingly false representation, and by its terms it reaches only solicitation that induces a change of residence. Section 973 is addressed to what is not said, and contains no relocation element and no knowledge element in its text: it directs that the advertisement or solicitation mention the dispute. Silence about a dispute is thus the subject of section 973 rather than of section 970(d), while a knowingly false denial of a dispute made to induce a move falls within section 970(d).

LABOR CODE SECTION 974 - VIOLATION OF SECTION 973 IS A MISDEMEANOR
Labor Code section 974 supplies the penalty for section 973. It provides that any person, or agent or officer of that person, who violates section 973 is guilty of a misdemeanor. The section is one sentence long. Unlike section 971, the penalty provision for section 970, section 974 does not itself state a fine range or a maximum term of imprisonment; it classifies the offense and no more. Section 974 also creates no civil remedy in its text, and the chapter contains no counterpart to the double-damages provision that section 972 supplies for violations of section 970.

PEOPLE V. SMITH - A SECTION 973 PROSECUTION, AND THE REJECTION OF A VAGUENESS CHALLENGE
People v. Smith (1955) 133 Cal.App.2d Supp. 777 is a reported decision arising from an actual prosecution under Labor Code section 973. The defendant was charged with inserting an advertisement in a Los Angeles newspaper soliciting persons to work for him while a strike, lockout, or other trade dispute was in active progress at his establishment, and with failing to state plainly and explicitly in the advertisement that such a dispute was in active progress. The trial court dismissed the action on the ground that section 973 was indefinite and uncertain. The reviewing court reversed. It held first that the dismissal exceeded the trial court's authority under Penal Code section 1385, and then held separately that section 973 is not invalid for uncertainty. As to the words "strike" and "lockout," the court said that they "are of such common use and their meaning, when applied to the subject of labor relations, with which this statute deals, is so plain, that their use in the statute cannot be held to introduce any uncertainty into it." The disposition was that "The judgment of dismissal is reversed, and the trial court is directed to retry the case."

PEOPLE V. SMITH ON THE PURPOSE OF SECTION 973
In rejecting the vagueness challenge, the court in People v. Smith stated the object it understood the Legislature to have had in enacting section 973. It wrote that "The Legislature was trying to protect workers against the form of misrepresentation of which there had been much complaint in the past, in which employers who had labor troubles sought employees without notifying those approached that such labor troubles existed." The court reasoned from that object to a reading of the section's two key phrases, concluding that it would be unreasonable to suppose that the labor troubles whose existence triggers the duty to speak differ from the labor troubles the employer is required to state, and adding: "We think they are not." The passage characterizes silence about a labor dispute as a "form of misrepresentation" - the same characterization the chapter heading carries - rather than as a distinct category of wrong.

PEOPLE V. SMITH ON "TRADE DISPUTE" AND THE LINK TO UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE CODE SECTION 1262
Asked to hold "trade dispute" and "labor disturbance" too indefinite for a penal statute, the court in People v. Smith looked to the use of "trade dispute" elsewhere in California law. It noted that the phrase came into the unemployment compensation statutes in 1935 and observed that "This provision is now in section 1262 of the Unemployment Insurance Code, in substantially the same form." Surveying the California Supreme Court decisions applying that unemployment insurance provision, the court concluded that "In all of these cases the term 'trade dispute' has been regarded as relating to the relations between employers and those who did or might work for them. It extends to contentions between employers and unions, even though no members of the union are then working for such employers." The effect of the reasoning is that the phrase in the hiring statute and the phrase in the unemployment benefits statute were read together, so that the same body of decisions bears on both.

A QUESTION PEOPLE V. SMITH EXPRESSLY LEFT OPEN
The court in People v. Smith closed its discussion by reserving a question it had not been required to decide. Having held the statute valid, it stated: "We are not considering the question whether the use in the complaint of the words 'trade dispute' where the statute uses the words 'labor disturbance' would impair the efficacy of the complaint to charge an offense." The complaint in that case had charged the defendant with failing to state that "a strike, lockout, or other trade dispute was in active progress," while the sentence of section 973 that prescribes what must be stated uses the words "a strike, lockout, or other labor disturbance exists." The court therefore declined to say whether a charging document that substitutes one of the statute's phrases for the other states an offense. No later decision resolving that reserved question was located.

BELKNAP V. HALE - STATE-LAW MISREPRESENTATION AND CONTRACT CLAIMS BY REPLACEMENTS HELD NOT PREEMPTED
Belknap itself concerned what a replacement may do when the promise that induced the hire is not kept. Replacements who had been offered and had accepted jobs described as permanent, and who were assured they would not be fired to accommodate returning strikers, were displaced when the strikers were reinstated; they sued the employer in state court for misrepresentation and breach of contract. The Court held the claims not preempted. It reasoned that "But when an employer attempts to exercise this very privilege by promising the replacements that they will not be discharged to make room for returning strikers, it surely does not follow that the employer's otherwise valid promises of permanent employment are nullified by federal law and its otherwise actionable misrepresentations may not be pursued." It distinguished the parties to the labor dispute from those outside it: "It is one thing to hold that the federal law intended to leave the employer and the union free to use their economic weapons against one another, but is quite another to hold that either the employer or the union is also free to injure innocent third parties without regard to the normal rules of law governing those relationships." Justice Brennan concurred in the judgment and Justice Blackmun wrote separately; three Justices dissented, taking the view that both claims were preempted.

A FEDERAL CRIMINAL PROVISION ADDRESSED TO MOVING WORKERS INTO A LABOR CONTROVERSY - 18 U.S.C. § 1231
A federal criminal statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1231, is captioned "Transportation of strikebreakers" and addresses the movement of persons across state lines in connection with a labor controversy. Its first paragraph reaches whoever "willfully transports in interstate or foreign commerce any person who is employed or is to be employed for the purpose of obstructing or interfering by force or threats with (1) peaceful picketing by employees during any labor controversy affecting wages, hours, or conditions of labor, or (2) the exercise by employees of any of the rights of self-organization or collective bargaining." A second paragraph reaches whoever "is knowingly transported or travels in interstate or foreign commerce for any of the purposes enumerated in this section." The penalty is a fine under title 18 or imprisonment of not more than two years, or both, and the section states that it "shall not apply to common carriers." On the face of the text the offense turns on a purpose of obstructing or interfering "by force or threats," so the section is not addressed to the ordinary recruitment or transportation of replacement workers, and its caption is broader than its operative language.

expectedJSON.body: Sections 970 and 973 sit in the same Labor Code chapter and both speak to labor disputes, but they operate differently. Section 970 prohibits influencing, persuading, or engaging a person to change residence for work "through or by means of knowingly false representations" about any of four listed subjects, the fourth of which, subdivision (d), is the existence or nonexistence of a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute affecting the work and pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last engaged in that labor. expectedJSON.body: Belknap itself concerned what a replacement may do when the promise that induced the hire is not kept. Replacements who had been offered and had accepted jobs described as permanent, and who were assured they would not be fired to accommodate returning strikers, were displaced when the strikers were reinstated; they sued the employer in state court for misrepresentation and breach of contract. The Court held the claims not preempted. It reasoned that "But when an employer attempts to exercise this very privilege by promising the replacements that they will not be discharged to make room for returning strikers, it surely does not follow that the employer's otherwise valid promises of permanent employment are nullified by federal law and its otherwise actionable misrepresentations may not be pursued." It distinguished the parties to the labor dispute from those outside it: "It is one thing to hold that the federal law intended to leave the employer and the union free to use their economic weapons against one another, but is quite another to hold that either the employer or the union is also free to injure innocent third parties without regard to the normal rules of law governing those relationships." Justice Brennan concurred in the judgment and Justice Blackmun wrote separately; three Justices dissented, taking the view that both claims were preempted.
